entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Brethren (also known as Church of the Brethren in the US, originally called 'Dunkers' or 'Dunkards' from their practice of trine immersion baptism), founded in 1708 in Schwarzenau, Germany by Alexander Mack and seven others — drawing on Anabaptist, Pietist, and Reformed traditions — is one of the historic peace churches alongside Quakers and Mennonites, whose commitment to nonresistance, adult baptism, simplicity, and refusal of oaths has shaped distinctive pacifist Christian communities for over three centuries.

The Brethren movement emerged from the Radical Pietist milieu of early 18th-century Germany: disillusioned with established churches and influenced by the Pietist emphasis on inner spiritual transformation, Mack's group rejected infant baptism, church-state alliances, and military service. Facing persecution in Germany, most Brethren emigrated to Pennsylvania beginning in 1719 — joining the Mennonites and Quakers in creating colonial Pennsylvania's extraordinary concentration of peace church communities.

In America, the Brethren diversified over centuries: the Church of the Brethren (mainstream, headquartered in Elgin, Illinois) maintains its historic peace church identity; the Brethren Church and other groups represent various 19th-century separations. The denomination was central to Conscientious Objector provision recognition in World War I and II, and the Brethren Volunteer Service (1948) — one of America's oldest voluntary service programs — influenced the later creation of the Peace Corps. The Brethren contribution to American religious pluralism and civil conscientious objection frameworks has been disproportionate to their relatively small numbers (about 130,000 members).

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Brethren — one of the historic peace churches, shaping American conscientious objection law, founding a voluntary service program that influenced the Peace Corps, and maintaining a 315-year tradition of nonresistance and simplicity — have had an outsized influence on American civil religious pluralism relative to their small numbers.
